name: Merchant cash advance (MCA)
title: Merchant cash advance (MCA): Formula and Worked Example
description: A merchant cash advance provides funding against future business receipts under a contract. A factor-based remittance total and a sales holdback percentage answer different cash-flow questions.
definition: A merchant cash advance provides funding against future business receipts under a contract. A factor-based remittance total and a sales holdback percentage answer different cash-flow questions.
explanation: A factor rate of 1.30 on a $50,000 advance means $65,000 of contracted remittances. With a $1,500 withheld fee, the business receives $48,500 and pays $16,500 more than that net funding. Annualized cost also depends on the actual remittance dates.
formula: Total remittances = advance × factor. Net funding = advance − withheld fees. Effective annual r solves net funding = Σ remittance / (1+r)^(calendar days/365).
formulaNote: One USD factor-based advance; one fee withheld at funding; all remittances later than funding. Fixed count or constant eligible-sales/holdback scenario, actual calendar dates and Actual/365 effective annual IRR. At most 1,000 remittances /3,650 days; IRR above 1,000,000% flagged. No legal APR, state disclosures, variable-sales forecast, extra fees, refinancing or actual contract reconciliation.

example.title: Reconcile gross advance, withheld fee and total cash cost
example.intro: advance: 50000; factor: 1.3; withheld_fees: 1500; funding_date: 2026-12-01; first_debit: 2026-12-02; calendar: Weekdays (Mon–Fri only); remittances: 130
steps: Cash cost = 65,000 − 48,500 = 16,500; the factor markup alone is only 15,000.
example.answer: Total financing cash cost above net funding: 16,500.00 under these assumptions.
example.assumptions: One USD factor-based advance; one fee withheld at funding; all remittances later than funding. pitfall.title: Keep the comparison basis consistent
pitfall.text: A 1.30 factor is not a 30% annual rate. Timing, amortizing remittances and fees withheld from proceeds change the effective annual cash-flow rate. A constant-sales scenario is not a guaranteed payoff date.

name: Backdoor Roth IRA and pro-rata basis
title: Backdoor Roth IRA and pro-rata basis: Formula and Worked Example
description: A backdoor Roth strategy generally involves a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution followed by a Roth conversion. The ordinary taxable split depends on the person’s aggregate IRA basis and included IRA pool, not solely the new account.
definition: A backdoor Roth strategy generally involves a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution followed by a Roth conversion. The ordinary taxable split depends on the person’s aggregate IRA basis and included IRA pool, not solely the new account.
explanation: A backdoor Roth conversion is not automatically tax-free. With $7,500 established nondeductible basis, $92,500 left in included IRAs at year end and $7,500 converted, the ordinary pool is $100,000. Only $562.50 of the conversion is nontaxable; $6,937.50 is taxable.
formula: Eligible basis = prior basis + current-year nondeductible contributions − following-year portion. Fraction = min(1, eligible basis / (year-end IRA values + included rollovers + other distributions + conversions)). Remaining basis = total basis − both nontaxable allocations.
formulaNote: U.S. 2026 ordinary individual traditional-IRA pro-rata allocation using established nondeductible basis, aggregated included December 31 IRA values, eligible outstanding IRA-to-IRA rollovers, conversions and other included distributions. Following-year contributions excluded from current allocation but retained in basis. Published 2026 Form 8606; 2025 instructions for context. No contribution/deduction eligibility engine, special adjustments, inherited/mega-backdoor plan, penalties, five-year withdrawal or full-return calculation.

example.title: Allocate basis across existing IRA balances
example.intro: case_scope: Ordinary case; basis confirmed; prior_basis: 0; current_nondeductible: 7500; year_end_iras: 92500; outstanding_rollovers: 0; converted: 7500; assumed_rate: 24
example.answer: Taxable portion of 2026 Roth conversions: 6,937.50 under these assumptions.

pitfall.title: Keep the comparison basis consistent
pitfall.text: A separate new IRA does not isolate nondeductible basis from the person’s other included IRAs. Contribution tax year and calendar conversion year can differ; a contribution made in early 2027 for 2026 does not shelter a 2026 conversion in this ordinary calculation.
